title: The filesystem, absolute and relative paths

videos.script: Ask somebody where they keep a file and they will tell you a story. It is in the folder I made for the project, the one inside documents, I think. On Linux there is no story. There is an address, it starts with a slash, and it is the same address from every program, every account and every machine that has the disk mounted. {{address}} That is what this lesson is: the tree, and how to say where you are in it. And the reason it comes third, before permissions and before processes, is that nearly everything else needs it. A service that will not start is usually looking at a path. A permission that was denied was denied on a path. A backup that ran all night into nothing was writing to a directory that was supposed to be a disk. {{why}} Two ideas carry the whole hour. The first is that there is one tree, one root, and everything hangs off it — no drive letters, no separate universes. You saw that in lesson one. The second is the one people trip on for weeks: a path either starts at the root or it starts where you are standing, and the leading slash is the entire difference. {{two}} We will walk the standard directories and say what each is actually for. We will read a long listing field by field, which is the densest line in this course and the one you will look at a thousand times. We will find things, match things, link things, and open an archive without googling the three letters. {{tour}} And at the end you should be able to look at any path on any Linux machine and say, without running anything, roughly what is in it and why it is there. {{title}}

No slides. A real machine, and we walk its root directory from the top. {{open}} Here it is. Eighteen or so entries, and the four that are arrows rather than directories are the first thing worth noticing — bin, lib, sbin and lib64 all point into usr. That is not this machine being odd; that is every modern distribution, and lesson two told you why. {{root}} Start with etc. Configuration, for the whole machine, and it is all text. A thousand and sixty-five entries in bin, seventy-five in etc — and every one of those etc entries is something you can open with cat. {{etc}} Now var. Things that change while the machine runs. Log is the one you will live in. {{var}} Usr. What was installed. Bin is the programs, share is data that does not care what processor you are on, and local is the one to remember: software you installed by hand, kept where the package manager will not fight you for it. {{usr}} Home. One directory per person. {{home}} And then the two that are not really directories at all. Proc — ask it the uptime and it answers with two numbers that did not exist until you asked. {{proc}} And dev. Null, zero, urandom, tty. Character devices, and the first column of that listing starts with a c rather than a dash, which is the file type telling you these are not files. {{dev}} Last thing. Watch what happens when I list the same path two ways. {{bin-two}} With minus l, ls showed me the link. With a slash on the end, it showed me what the link points at. Same seven characters typed, two different questions asked, and the difference is a habit worth building tonight rather than on a Tuesday afternoon in production.

That is the tree. {{open}} Three things to carry out of it. The first is the slash at the front. A path with one starts at the root and means the same thing typed anywhere; a path without one starts where you are standing and means something different in every directory. Every path bug you will write for the next month is that sentence, ignored. {{slash}} The second is that the long listing is readable. Type, permissions, links, owner, group, size, time, name — eight fields, and you now know what each one is for. Permissions get their own lesson next, and you will arrive there already able to see them. {{listing}} The third is the one that is really about the shell rather than the tree. A star is expanded before the command runs. The command never sees your star; it sees the list of names the shell handed it. That is why rm star is not a command that deletes everything, it is a command that is handed everything. {{glob}} And the honest warning. Nothing in this lesson asks you if you are sure. Copy over a file that existed and it is gone, with no message, no bin to recover it from, and no undo. That is not a design oversight — it is the same contract that lets you do the same thing to ten thousand files. The habit that costs nothing is to look before you press enter, and to run the destructive thing as ls first. {{careful}} Next lesson is the one that explains why half of what you tried was refused. Permissions: twelve bits, three audiences, and a denial you will be able to name out loud. {{next}} Before that, the drill. Sixteen of them, and most are a path you have to resolve in your head.
